```{r}
set.seed(100)
```

## Hypothesis Test and Type-I Error

::: {.callout title="Definition 25.1"}
A **hypothesis test** is used to test the plausibility of a **null hypothesis** about a parameter $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, $H_0: \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \Theta_0$, vs an **alternative hypothesis**, $H_A: \boldsymbol{\theta} \notin \Theta_0$, using a test statistic $T(\boldsymbol{X})$. If the distribution of $T(\boldsymbol{X})$ under the null hypothesis is known, then we can define a **rejection region** $R$ such that:

$$P(T(\boldsymbol{X}) \in R | \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \Theta_0) = \alpha$$

where $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ is the **Type-I Error** or **significance level**, the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when the null hypothesis is true.
:::

## P-Value

::: {.callout title="Definition 25.2"}
A **p-value** is the probability of observing a test statistic $T(\boldsymbol{X})$ as extreme or more extreme than the observed value $T(\boldsymbol{x})$, given that the null hypothesis is true. The following shows how to calculate p-values for different types of alternative hypotheses:

$$
\begin{align}
H_A: \mu \neq \mu_0 &\Rightarrow P\left(T(\boldsymbol{X}) \geq |T(\boldsymbol{x})| \Big| \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \Theta_0 \right) = \text{p} \\ \\
H_A: \mu < \mu_0 &\Rightarrow P\left(T(\boldsymbol{X}) \leq T(\boldsymbol{x}) \Big| \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \Theta_0 \right) = \text{p}\\ \\
H_A: \mu > \mu_0 &\Rightarrow P\left(T(\boldsymbol{X}) \geq T(\boldsymbol{x}) \Big| \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \Theta_0 \right) = \text{p}
\end{align}
$$
:::

If $\text{p} < \alpha$, then this implies that $T(\boldsymbol{x}) \in R$ and we would reject the null hypothesis. In other words, "if $\text{p}$ is low, reject the null" or "if $\text{p}$ is low, the null must go".

## Hypothesis Test for Population Mean (Two-Tailed, Known Variance)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 25.1"}
Let $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ be independent and identically distributed normal random variables with unknown mean $\mu$ and known standard deviation $\sigma$. Assume we want to test the hypothesis $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ vs $H_A: \mu \neq \mu_0$ and we want the Type-I error rate to be no larger than $\alpha$. Then we would reject $H_0$ when the following was true:

$$
\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} < z_{\alpha/2} \quad \text{ or } \quad \frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} > z_{1-\alpha/2}
$$

More succinctly, we can reject $H_0$ when $\left|\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \right| > z_{1-\alpha/2}$
:::

If the underlying distribution is unknown, we can still apply this if $n \geq 30$.

## Hypothesis Test for Population Mean (Two-Tailed, Known Variance, Proof)

Under the null hypothesis, $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ are distributed normally with mean $\mu = \mu_0$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. Then $\frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim N(0, 1)$. Thus, if the null hypothesis is true, the probability of rejecting the null using this rejection region is:

$$
P\left(\frac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} < z_{\alpha/2}\right) + P\left(\frac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} > z_{1-\alpha/2}\right) = P\left(\left|\frac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \right| > z_{1-\alpha/2}\right) = \alpha
$$

If the underlying distribution is unknown, we can still apply this if $n \geq 30$.

## Hypothesis Test for Population Mean (Left-Tailed, Known Variance)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 25.2"}
Let $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ be independent and identically distributed normal random variables with unknown mean $\mu$ and known standard deviation $\sigma$. Assume we want to test the hypothesis $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ vs $H_A: \mu < \mu_0$ and we want the Type-I error rate to be no larger than $\alpha$. Then we would reject $H_0$ when the following was true:

$$
\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} < z_{\alpha}
$$
:::

Again, under the null hypothesis, we have that $\frac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim N(0, 1)$. Thus, if the null is true, the probability of rejecting it would be:

$$
P\left(\frac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} < z_{\alpha}\right) = \alpha
$$

If the underlying distribution is unknown, we can still apply this if $n \geq 30$.

## Hypothesis Test for Population Mean (Right-Tailed, Known Variance)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 25.3"}
Let $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ be independent and identically distributed normal random variables with unknown mean $\mu$ and known standard deviation $\sigma$. Assume we want to test the hypothesis $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ vs $H_A: \mu > \mu_0$ and we want the Type-I error rate to be no larger than $\alpha$. Then we would reject $H_0$ when the following was true:

$$
\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} > z_{1-\alpha}
$$
:::

Again, under the null hypothesis, we have that $\frac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim N(0, 1)$. Thus, if the null is true, the probability of rejecting it would be:

$$
P\left(\frac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} > z_{1-\alpha}\right) = \alpha
$$

If the underlying distribution is unknown, we can still apply this if $n \geq 30$.

## P-Value for Population Mean (Two-Tailed, Known Variance)

For a two-tailed test involving the population mean with known variance ($H_A: \mu \neq \mu_0$), the p-value would be computed as follows:

$$
P\left(\frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \geq \left|\frac{\bar{x}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \right| \Bigg| \mu = \mu_0\right)
$$

In words, this is literally the probability of getting a test-statistic as larger or larger than what we observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true.

## P-Value for Population Mean (Left-Tailed, Known Variance)

For a left-tailed test involving the population mean with known variance ($H_A: \mu < \mu_0$), the p-value would be computed as follows:

$$
P\left(\frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \leq \frac{\bar{x}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \Bigg| \mu = \mu_0\right)
$$

## P-Value for Population Mean (Right-Tailed, Known Variance)

For a right-tailed test involving the population mean with known variance. ($H_A: \mu > \mu_0$), the p-value would be computed as follows:

$$
P\left(\frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \geq \frac{\bar{x}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \Bigg| \mu = \mu_0\right)
$$

## Hypothesis Test for Population Mean (Two-Tailed, Unknown Variance)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 25.4"}
Let $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ be independent and identically distributed normal random variables with unknown mean $\mu$ and unknown standard deviation $\sigma$. Assume we want to test the hypothesis $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ vs $H_A: \mu \neq \mu_0$ and we want the Type-I error rate to be no larger than $\alpha$. Then we would reject $H_0$ when the following was true:

$$
\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}} < t_{n-1, \alpha/2} \quad \text{ or } \quad \frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}} > t_{n-1, 1-\alpha/2}
$$

More succinctly, we can reject $H_0$ when $\left|\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}} \right| > t_{n-1, 1-\alpha/2}$
:::

The proofs for this are very similar to the case when the standard deviation is known. If the underlying distribution is unknown, we can still apply this if $n \geq 30$.

## Hypothesis Test for Population Mean (Left-Tailed, Unknown Variance)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 25.5"}
Let $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ be independent and identically distributed normal random variables with unknown mean $\mu$ and unknown standard deviation $\sigma$. Assume we want to test the hypothesis $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ vs $H_A: \mu < \mu_0$ and we want the Type-I error rate to be no larger than $\alpha$. Then we would reject $H_0$ when the following was true:

$$
\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}} < t_{n-1,\alpha}
$$
:::

The proof is similar to the case where the variance is known. If the underlying distribution is unknown, we can still apply this if $n \geq 30$.

## Hypothesis Test for Population Mean (Right-Tailed, Unknown Variance)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 25.6"}
Let $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ be independent and identically distributed normal random variables with unknown mean $\mu$ and unknown standard deviation $\sigma$. Assume we want to test the hypothesis $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ vs $H_A: \mu > \mu_0$ and we want the Type-I error rate to be no larger than $\alpha$. Then we would reject $H_0$ when the following was true:

$$
\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}} > t_{n-1,1-\alpha}
$$
:::

The proof is similar to the case where the variance is known. If the underlying distribution is unknown, we can still apply this if $n \geq 30$.

## P-Value for Population Mean (Two-Tailed, Unknown Variance)

For a two-tailed test involving the population mean with unknown variance ($H_A: \mu \neq \mu_0$), the p-value would be computed as follows:

$$
P\left(\frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{S/\sqrt{n}} \geq \left|\frac{\bar{x}-\mu}{s/\sqrt{n}} \right| \Bigg| \mu = \mu_0\right)
$$

## P-Value for Population Mean (Left-Tailed, Unknown Variance)

For a left-tailed test involving the population mean with unknown variance ($H_A: \mu < \mu_0$), the p-value would be computed as follows:

$$
P\left(\frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{S/\sqrt{n}} \leq \frac{\bar{x}-\mu}{s/\sqrt{n}} \Bigg| \mu = \mu_0\right)
$$

## P-Value for Population Mean (Right-Tailed, Unknown Variance)

For a left-tailed test involving the population mean with unknown variance ($H_A: \mu > \mu_0$), the p-value would be computed as follows:

$$
P\left(\frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{S/\sqrt{n}} \geq \frac{\bar{x}-\mu}{s/\sqrt{n}} \Bigg| \mu = \mu_0\right)
$$

## Ex: Batteries (1)

::: {.callout title="Example 25.1"}
Historically, the average weight for a certain type of battery has been 51 grams, but it believed that the weight has increased. A random sample of 40 batteries is selected, and their average weight is found to be 51.5 grams. It is known that the weight of these batteries follows a normal distribution with a standard deviation of 1.8 grams.

Assume a significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$. What test-statistic would we use for this test and what critical value is used to define the rejection region?
:::

. . .

-   $H_0: \mu = 51$
-   $H_A: \mu > 51$

This test would use a z-statistic since $\sigma$ is known

```{r, echo = TRUE}
alpha <- 0.05

cat("The critical value is: ", qnorm(1-alpha))
```

## Ex: Drug Recovery (1)

::: {.callout title="Example 25.2"}
In the past, the mean recovery time for a certain drug was 14 days. It is believed that the mean recovery time is different now. A random sample of 35 patients who took the drug had a mean recovery time of 13.5 days with a sample standard deviation of 2.5 days.

Assume a significance level of $\alpha = 0.01$. What test-statistic would we use for this test and what critical value is used to define the rejection region?
:::

. . .

-   $H_0: \mu = 14$
-   $H_A: \mu \neq 14$

This test would use a t-statistic since $\sigma$ is unknown.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 35
alpha <- 0.01

cat("The critical value is: ", qt(1-alpha/2, n-1))
```

## Ex: Sugar (1)

::: {.callout title="Example 25.3"}
In the past, the average sugar content for a fruit drink was 18 grams per bottle. It is believed the sugar content has decreased. A random sample of 50 bottles is tested, and the average sugar content is found to be 17.2 grams per bottle. Previous studies have shown that the population standard deviation is 3.2 grams.

Assume a significance level of $\alpha = 0.1$. What test-statistic would we use for this test and what critical value is used to define the rejection region?
:::

. . .

-   $H_0: \mu = 18$
-   $H_A: \mu < 18$

This test would use a z-statistic since $\sigma$ is known

```{r, echo = TRUE}
alpha <- 0.1

cat("The critical value is: ", qnorm(alpha))
```

## Ex: Batteries (2)

::: {.callout title="Example 25.4"}
Historically, the average weight for a certain type of battery has been 51 grams, but it is believed that the weight has increased. A random sample of 40 batteries is selected, and their average weight is found to be 51.5 grams. It is known that the weight of these batteries follows a normal distribution with a standard deviation of 1.8 grams.

Using a significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$, test the hypothesis that the true average weight has increased from 51 grams.
:::

. . .

-   $H_0: \mu = 51$
-   $H_A: \mu > 51$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 40
sigma <- 1.8
mu_0 <- 51
xbar <- 51.5
alpha <- 0.05
z_statistic <- (xbar-mu_0)/(sigma/sqrt(n))

cat("The z-statistic is: ", z_statistic, ", the critical value is: ", qnorm(1-alpha), ", and the p-value is: ", 1-pnorm(z_statistic), sep = "")
```

## Ex: Drug Recovery (2)

::: {.callout title="Example 25.5"}
In the past, the mean recovery time for a certain drug was 14 days. It is believed that the mean recovery time is different now. A random sample of 35 patients who took the drug had a mean recovery time of 13.5 days with a sample standard deviation of 2.5 days.

Using a significance level of $\alpha = 0.01$, test the hypothesis that the true mean recovery time is different from 13.5 days.
:::

. . .

-   $H_0: \mu = 14$
-   $H_A: \mu \neq 14$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 35
s <- 2.5
mu_0 <- 14
xbar <- 13.5
alpha <- 0.01
t_statistic <- (xbar-mu_0)/(s/sqrt(n))

cat("The t-statistic is: ", t_statistic, ", the critical value is: ", qt(1-alpha/2, n-1), ", and the p-value is: ", 2*pt(-abs(t_statistic), n-1), sep = "")
```

## Ex: Sugar (2)

::: {.callout title="Example 25.6"}
In the past, the average sugar content for a fruit drink was 18 grams per bottle. It is believed that this has decreased. A random sample of 50 bottles is tested, and the average sugar content is found to be 17.2 grams per bottle. Previous studies have shown that the population standard deviation is 3.2 grams.

Using a significance level of $\alpha = 0.1$, test the hypothesis that the true average sugar content has decreased from 18 grams.
:::

. . .

-   $H_0: \mu = 18$
-   $H_A: \mu < 18$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 50
sigma <- 3.2
mu_0 <- 18
xbar <- 17.2
alpha <- 0.1
z_statistic <- (xbar-mu_0)/(sigma/sqrt(n))

cat("The z-statistic is: ", z_statistic, ", the critical value is: ", qnorm(alpha), ", and the p-value is: ", pnorm(z_statistic), sep = "")
```

## Ex: Commute

::: {.callout title="Example 25.7"}
A city planner states that the average commute time is in a city 32 minutes, but you believe that it is larger than that. You collect a random sample of 40 commute times and find the sample mean is 32.8 minutes with a sample standard deviation of 6.8 minutes.

Using a significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$, test the hypothesis that the true average commute time is greater than 32 minutes.
:::

. . .

-   $H_0: \mu = 32$
-   $H_A: \mu > 32$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 40
s <- 6.8
mu_0 <- 32
xbar <- 32.8
alpha <- 0.05
t_statistic <- (xbar-mu_0)/(s/sqrt(n))

cat("The t-statistic is: ", t_statistic, ", the critical value is: ", qt(1-alpha, n-1), ", and the p-value is: ", 1-pt(t_statistic, n-1), sep = "")
```

## Ex: Fuel

::: {.callout title="Example 25.8"}
An airline believes that the average fuel consumption for a flight is 3800 gallons. However, they've been told there is a chance it is different than this and they'd like to test that. From historical data, the standard deviation of fuel consumption is known to be 250 gallons per flight. A random sample of 36 flights is selected. The mean fuel consumption is found to be 3900 gallons.

Using a significance level of $\alpha = 0.01$, test the hypothesis that the true mean fuel consumption is different from 3800 gallons.
:::

. . .

-   $H_0: \mu = 3800$
-   $H_A: \mu \neq 3800$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 36
sigma <- 250
mu_0 <- 3800
xbar <- 3900
alpha <- 0.01
z_statistic <- (xbar-mu_0)/(sigma/sqrt(n))

cat("The z-statistic is: ", z_statistic, ", the critical value is: ", qnorm(1-alpha/2), ", and the p-value is: ", 2*pnorm(-abs(z_statistic)), sep = "")
```

## Ex: Sleep

::: {.callout title="Example 25.9"}
A university claims that the average student sleeps 7 hours a night. You believe students get less sleep on average. A random sample of 50 students is surveyed, and their average sleep duration is found to be 6.7 hours per night with a sample standard deviation of 1.2 hours.

Using a significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$, test the hypothesis that the true average sleep duration is less than 7 hours.
:::

. . .

-   $H_0: \mu = 7$
-   $H_A: \mu < 7$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 50
s <- 1.2
mu_0 <- 7
xbar <- 6.7
alpha <- 0.05
t_statistic <- (xbar-mu_0)/(s/sqrt(n))

cat("The t-statistic is: ", t_statistic, ", the critical value is: ", qt(alpha, n-1), ", and the p-value is: ", pt(t_statistic, n-1), sep = "")
```

## Ex: Fertilizer

Given a set of observations with unknown mean and unknown standard deviation, we can use the `t.test` function in R to perform a hypothesis test for the population mean.

::: {.callout title="Example 25.10"}
A researcher is studying the effects of a new fertilizer on plant growth. They believe that before using this fertilizer that the average growth was 22 centimeters. However, they believe that it is greater now that they are using this new fertilizer. They measure the height (in cm) of 10 randomly selected plants after four weeks of growth:

```{r, echo = TRUE}
growth <- c(22.4, 21.8, 23.1, 24.0, 22.7, 23.5, 21.9, 22.6, 23.3, 22.1)
```

The researcher assumes that plant heights follow a normal distribution. Using a significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$, perform a hypothesis test to test the hypothesis that the average growth has increased.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- length(growth)
t_statistic <- (mean(growth)-22)/(sd(growth)/sqrt(n))

cat("The t-statistic is: ", t_statistic, ", the critical value is: ", qt(1-0.05, n-1), ", and the p-value is: ", 1-pt(t_statistic, n-1), sep = "")
```

## Ex: Fertilizer, Continued

::: {.callout title="Example 25.10 (Continued)"}
A researcher is studying the effects of a new fertilizer on plant growth. They believe that before using this fertilizer that the average growth was 22 centimeters. However, they believe that it is greater now that they are using this new fertilizer. They measure the height (in cm) of 10 randomly selected plants after four weeks of growth:

```{r, echo = TRUE}
growth <- c(22.4, 21.8, 23.1, 24.0, 22.7, 23.5, 21.9, 22.6, 23.3, 22.1)
```

The researcher assumes that plant heights follow a normal distribution. Using a significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$, perform a hypothesis test to test the hypothesis that the average growth has increased.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
t.test(growth, alternative = "greater", mu = 22, conf.level = 0.95)
```

## Ex: Break Times

::: {.callout title="Example 25.11"}
A company claims the average time (in minutes) that employees spend on breaks is 17 minutes, but you believe it is less than that. A random sample of 35 employees is selected, and the following break times are recorded:

```{r, echo = TRUE}
breaks <- c(12, 15, 18, 14, 16, 20, 19, 14, 13, 17, 18, 16, 19, 21, 15, 13, 14,
            16, 17, 18, 22, 23, 19, 15, 14, 12, 16, 18, 19, 17, 20, 21, 15, 14, 13)
```

Using a significance level of $\alpha = 0.01$, perform a hypothesis test to test the hypothesis that the average break time is less than 17 minutes.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
t.test(breaks, alternative = "less", mu = 17, conf.level = 0.99)
```

## Ex: Heart Rates

::: {.callout title="Example 25.12"}
Historical data at a hospital suggests that the average heart rate (in beats per minute) of patients recovering from a certain surgery is 75. However, it is believed that it might be different now. A random sample of 12 patients is selected, and their recorded heart rates are:

```{r, echo = TRUE}
rates <- c(72, 75, 78, 80, 76, 79, 81, 74, 77, 73, 76, 78)
```

It is assumed that the heart rates follow a normal distribution. Using a significance level of $\alpha = 0.1$, perform a hypothesis test to test the hypothesis that average heart rate is different from what it was.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
t.test(rates, alternative = "two.sided", mu = 75, conf.level = 0.9)
```

## Ex: Exam Scores

::: {.callout title="Example 25.13"}
A professor is analyzing the scores of students on a recent statistics exam. A random sample of 40 student scores is obtained:

```{r, echo = TRUE}
scores <- c(72, 85, 90, 78, 81, 76, 84, 89, 91, 95, 87, 73, 88, 77, 82, 86, 80, 
            83, 85, 79, 94, 92, 75, 78, 82, 84, 90, 88, 87, 85, 81, 79, 77, 86,
            92, 89, 90, 91, 80, 83)
```

The past average score was 85, but the professor believes it has decreased since then. Using a significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$, perform a hypothesis test to test that the average score has decreased.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
t.test(scores, alternative = "less", mu = 85, conf.level = 0.95)
```
